title: Hidden from the wise (Luke 10:21–24)
hookLine: Jesus rejoices that simple people understand

cards: The Gospels show Jesus weeping, sighing, angry at injustice, tired enough to sleep through a storm. They seldom say outright that he was joyful. So these four verses stand out.
The seventy have just come back buzzing with stories, and Luke says: "In that hour Jesus rejoiced in spirit."

The Greek verb is stronger than the English: exulting, overjoyed, the same family of words Mary used when she sang that her spirit rejoiced in God. What could make him that happy? Not who you'd expect.

teach.h: HID FROM THE WISE AND PRUDENT.
teach.b: In the King James words: "I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes: even so, Father; for so it seemed good in thy sight."
Babes, in Greek nepioi, means little children, infants. Not the experts, not the people with the best schooling or the highest positions.
Luke never tells us who the seventy were, only that they went out with no purse and no bag, and they've just seen what many learned people missed.
Jesus isn't against learning; Luke opens his Gospel saying he investigated everything carefully.

teach.h: THE DOOR YOU COME IN BY.
teach.b: The point is the door you come in by. Some things you don't grasp by being clever. You grasp them the way a child does: by trusting, by receiving, by not pretending you already know.
The people who are sure they understand can find the door closed precisely because they're sure.

teach.h: PROPHETS AND KINGS DESIRED TO SEE.
teach.b: Then Jesus turns to his disciples privately: "Blessed are the eyes which see the things that ye see: For I tell you, that many prophets and kings have desired to see those things which ye see, and have not seen them."

teach.h: BLESSED ARE THE EYES WHICH SEE THE THINGS THAT YE SEE.
teach.b: Isaiah, David, all the great names longed to see this, and the ones who got to see it are ordinary people from Galilee.
It's a warm reversal, and it fits Luke's whole Gospel: the shepherds before the priests, the widow before the rich, the child set beside him. The ones who receive are the ones who know they need to.

how: Many Christians treasure Luke 10:21 as a reminder that faith is open to everyone, and teachers of prayer across traditions often speak of receiving God like a child.

games.q: what's inside Luke 10:21–24 — tap the pairs.
p: desired to see, and did not

s: the Gospels seldom say outright that Jesus rejoiced
Luke 10:21 is one of the few places.
he's speaking of how things are received: like a child, trusting, not pretending to know.
Jesus said kings and prophets had longed to see what the disciples saw

games.q: your followers, ordinary people sent out with no purse and no bag, have just understood what experts missed. how do you respond?
o: tell them not to get proud.
rejoice, and thank the Father for revealing it to little children.
send them to study with the experts.
games.why: Jesus rejoices in spirit and thanks the Father for hiding these things from the wise and revealing them to babes.

practice: Think of the people who taught you the most important things, not from a stage but by how they lived: a grandmother who prayed while she cooked, a child who forgave quickly, a coworker with no title who always knew the right thing to do, someone with a disability or a hard life who sees what others miss.
Let one face come, and ask what they understood that cleverness couldn't teach. If you pray, give thanks for your unexpected teachers; if you don't, simply honor them.

wordCard.voice: Nepioi, Greek for little children, infants: Jesus rejoices that what the clever missed has been revealed to little children, ordinary people who simply received it.

orig.note: Greek: little children, infants. the "babes" to whom these things are revealed.

carryVoice: Your line: revealed to babes. Some things are received, not figured out. See you tomorrow.
